\(\angle\)RHD and \(\angle\)DHP form a linear pair, because R-H-P are collinear on line RP.
\(\therefore \angle\)RHD \(= 180^\circ - \angle\)DHP \(= 180^\circ - 85^\circ = 95^\circ\)

\(\angle\)PHG and \(\angle\)DHP form a linear pair, because D-H-G are collinear on the transversal DK.
\(\therefore \angle\)PHG \(= 180^\circ - 85^\circ = 95^\circ\)

Line RP \(\parallel\) line MS and line DK is their transversal.
\(\angle\)DHP and \(\angle\)HGS are corresponding angles.
Corresponding angles formed by a transversal of two parallel lines are congruent.
\(\therefore \angle\)HGS \(= \angle\)DHP \(= 85^\circ\)

\(\angle\)MGK and \(\angle\)HGS are opposite angles formed by the two intersecting lines MS and DK, so they are congruent.
\(\therefore \angle\)MGK \(= \angle\)HGS \(= 85^\circ\)
(\(\angle\)HGS is \(85^\circ\) by the corresponding-angles property, as found in part (iii).)

The angle of \(110^\circ\) and \(\angle a\) form a linear pair.
\(\therefore \angle a = 180^\circ - 110^\circ = 70^\circ\)
Line \(p \parallel\) line \(q\) and line \(l\) is their transversal, and \(\angle a\) and \(\angle\)b are corresponding angles.
\(\therefore \angle\)b \(= \angle a = 70^\circ\)
The angle of \(115^\circ\) and \(\angle\)d form a linear pair.
\(\therefore \angle\)d \(= 180^\circ - 115^\circ = 65^\circ\)
Line \(p \parallel\) line \(q\) and line \(m\) is their transversal, and \(\angle\)c and the angle of \(115^\circ\) are corresponding angles.
\(\therefore \angle\)c \(= 115^\circ\)
So \(\angle a = 70^\circ\), \(\angle\)b \(= 70^\circ\), \(\angle\)c \(= 115^\circ\), \(\angle\)d \(= 65^\circ\).

Line \(l \parallel\) line \(m\) and line \(p\) is their transversal.
The given angle of \(45^\circ\) and \(\angle a\) are interior angles on the same side of the transversal, so they are supplementary.
\(\therefore \angle a = 180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135^\circ\)
\(\angle a\) and \(\angle\)b are opposite angles formed by intersecting lines \(m\) and \(p\).
\(\therefore \angle\)b \(= \angle a = 135^\circ\)
Line \(n \parallel\) line \(p\) and line \(m\) is their transversal, and \(\angle\)b and \(\angle\)c are corresponding angles.
\(\therefore \angle\)c \(= \angle\)b \(= 135^\circ\)
So \(\angle a = \angle\)b \(= \angle\)c \(= 135^\circ\).

**Given :** ray QP \(\parallel\) ray YX and ray QR \(\parallel\) ray YZ.
**To prove :** \(\angle\)PQR \(\cong \angle\)XYZ.
**Construction :** Let ray YX, produced if necessary, meet ray QR at point T.
**Proof :** ray QP \(\parallel\) ray YX and line QR is their transversal.
\(\therefore \angle\)PQR \(\cong \angle\)XTR ..... corresponding angles ..... (I)
ray QR \(\parallel\) ray YZ, that is line QT \(\parallel\) line YZ, and line XY is their transversal.
\(\therefore \angle\)XTR \(\cong \angle\)XYZ ..... corresponding angles ..... (II)
From (I) and (II),
\(\angle\)PQR \(\cong \angle\)XYZ
That is, if the arms of two angles are parallel to each other, the angles are congruent.

The angle of \(105^\circ\) in the figure is \(\angle\)BRT, and \(\angle\)ART and \(\angle\)BRT form a linear pair on line AB.
\(\therefore \angle\)ART \(= 180^\circ - 105^\circ = 75^\circ\)

Line AB \(\parallel\) line CD and line PQ is their transversal.
\(\angle\)ART and \(\angle\)CTQ are corresponding angles.
\(\therefore \angle\)CTQ \(= \angle\)ART \(= 75^\circ\)  (from part (i))

\(\angle\)DTQ and \(\angle\)CTQ form a linear pair on line CD.
\(\therefore \angle\)DTQ \(= 180^\circ - 75^\circ = 105^\circ\)

\(\angle\)PRB and \(\angle\)ART are opposite angles formed by the intersecting lines AB and PQ.
\(\therefore \angle\)PRB \(= \angle\)ART \(= 75^\circ\)

\(x\) and \(y\) are the interior angles formed on the same side of the transversal \(l\) of line \(m\) and line \(n\).
If line \(m\) were parallel to line \(n\), these two angles would have to be supplementary, that is \(x + y = 180^\circ\).
Here \(x + y = 71^\circ + 108^\circ = 179^\circ\), and \(179^\circ \neq 180^\circ\).
\(\therefore\) **No**, the lines \(m\) and \(n\) are not parallel.
(The difference is only \(1^\circ\), so the lines look parallel in the figure - which is exactly why the test has to be applied rather than judged by eye.)

**Given :** \(\angle a \cong \angle\)b, where \(\angle a\) and \(\angle\)b are the angles formed by transversal \(n\) of line \(l\) and line \(m\).
**To prove :** line \(l \parallel\) line \(m\).
**Proof :** \(\angle a\) and \(\angle\)b are a pair of alternate angles formed by the transversal \(n\) of line \(l\) and line \(m\).
It is given that \(\angle a \cong \angle\)b.
If a pair of alternate angles formed by a transversal of two lines is congruent, then the two lines are parallel ..... alternate angles test.
\(\therefore\) line \(l \parallel\) line \(m\).

**Given :** \(\angle a \cong \angle\)b and \(\angle x \cong \angle y\).
**To prove :** line \(l \parallel\) line \(n\).
**Proof :** \(\angle a\) and \(\angle\)b are corresponding angles formed by transversal K of line \(l\) and line \(m\), and \(\angle a \cong \angle\)b is given.
\(\therefore\) line \(l \parallel\) line \(m\) ..... corresponding angles test ..... (I)
\(\angle x\) and \(\angle y\) are corresponding angles formed by their transversal of line \(m\) and line \(n\), and \(\angle x \cong \angle y\) is given.
\(\therefore\) line \(m \parallel\) line \(n\) ..... corresponding angles test ..... (II)
From (I) and (II), line \(l\) and line \(n\) are both parallel to line \(m\).
If two lines in a plane are parallel to a third line, then those two lines are parallel to each other ..... Corollary II.
\(\therefore\) line \(l \parallel\) line \(n\).

**Construction :** Draw ray CP through point C, parallel to ray BA, as the hint suggests.
Since ray BA \(\parallel\) ray DE is given and ray CP \(\parallel\) ray BA, we also have ray CP \(\parallel\) ray DE.
ray CP \(\parallel\) ray DE and seg CD is their transversal.
\(\therefore \angle\)PCD \(+ \angle\)CDE \(= 180^\circ\) ..... interior angles on the same side
\(\therefore \angle\)PCD \(= 180^\circ - 100^\circ = 80^\circ\)
Now \(\angle\)BCP \(= \angle\)BCD \(+ \angle\)DCP \(= 50^\circ + 80^\circ = 130^\circ\)
ray BA \(\parallel\) ray CP and seg BC is their transversal.
\(\therefore \angle\)ABC \(= \angle\)BCP ..... alternate angles
\(\therefore \angle\)ABC \(= 130^\circ\)

**Given :** ray AE \(\parallel\) ray BD; ray AF bisects \(\angle\)EAB and ray BC bisects \(\angle\)ABD.
**To prove :** line AF \(\parallel\) line BC.
**Proof :** ray AE \(\parallel\) ray BD and seg AB is their transversal. In the figure ray AE and ray BD point in opposite directions, so \(\angle\)EAB and \(\angle\)ABD are a pair of alternate angles.
\(\therefore \angle\)EAB \(= \angle\)ABD ..... alternate angles ..... (I)
ray AF bisects \(\angle\)EAB, so \(\angle\)FAB \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)EAB.
ray BC bisects \(\angle\)ABD, so \(\angle\)ABC \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)ABD.
Taking half of both sides of (I),
\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)EAB \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)ABD, that is \(\angle\)FAB \(= \angle\)ABC.
\(\angle\)FAB and \(\angle\)ABC are alternate angles formed by transversal AB of line AF and line BC, and they are congruent.
\(\therefore\) line AF \(\parallel\) line BC ..... alternate angles test.

**Given :** transversal EF of line AB and line CD meets them at P and Q; ray PR \(\parallel\) ray QS; ray PR bisects \(\angle\)BPQ and ray QS bisects \(\angle\)PQC.
**To prove :** line AB \(\parallel\) line CD.
**Proof :** ray PR \(\parallel\) ray QS and seg PQ is their transversal.
\(\therefore \angle\)RPQ \(= \angle\)PQS ..... alternate angles ..... (I)
ray PR bisects \(\angle\)BPQ, so \(\angle\)RPQ \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)BPQ.
ray QS bisects \(\angle\)PQC, so \(\angle\)PQS \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)PQC.
Substituting in (I),
\(\dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)BPQ \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)PQC
\(\therefore \angle\)BPQ \(= \angle\)PQC
\(\angle\)BPQ and \(\angle\)PQC are alternate angles formed by transversal EF of line AB and line CD, and they are congruent.
\(\therefore\) line AB \(\parallel\) line CD ..... alternate angles test.

Draw ray PQ and ray PR perpendicular to each other, so \(\angle\)QPR \(= 90^\circ\). Take point B in the interior of \(\angle\)QPR and point A in its exterior, on the far side of ray PQ, so that ray PB \(\perp\) ray PA, that is \(\angle\)APB \(= 90^\circ\).
Let \(\angle\)QPB \(= \theta\). Then, since ray PB is interior to \(\angle\)QPR,
\(\angle\)BPR \(= 90^\circ - \theta\), and \(\angle\)APQ \(= \angle\)APB \(- \angle\)QPB \(= 90^\circ - \theta\).
**A pair of complementary angles :** \(\angle\)QPB and \(\angle\)BPR, because \(\angle\)QPB \(+ \angle\)BPR \(= \theta + (90^\circ - \theta) = 90^\circ\).
(\(\angle\)APQ and \(\angle\)QPB is another such pair, for the same reason.)

Draw ray PQ and ray PR perpendicular to each other, so \(\angle\)QPR \(= 90^\circ\). Take point B in the interior of \(\angle\)QPR and point A in its exterior, on the far side of ray PQ, so that ray PB \(\perp\) ray PA, that is \(\angle\)APB \(= 90^\circ\).
Let \(\angle\)QPB \(= \theta\). Then, since ray PB is interior to \(\angle\)QPR,
\(\angle\)BPR \(= 90^\circ - \theta\), and \(\angle\)APQ \(= \angle\)APB \(- \angle\)QPB \(= 90^\circ - \theta\).
**A pair of supplementary angles :** \(\angle\)APB and \(\angle\)QPR, because each is \(90^\circ\) and \(90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ\).
(\(\angle\)APR and \(\angle\)... any angle completing it to a straight angle would also do; the simplest pair to name is the two given right angles.)

Draw ray PQ and ray PR perpendicular to each other, so \(\angle\)QPR \(= 90^\circ\). Take point B in the interior of \(\angle\)QPR and point A in its exterior, on the far side of ray PQ, so that ray PB \(\perp\) ray PA, that is \(\angle\)APB \(= 90^\circ\).
Let \(\angle\)QPB \(= \theta\). Then, since ray PB is interior to \(\angle\)QPR,
\(\angle\)BPR \(= 90^\circ - \theta\), and \(\angle\)APQ \(= \angle\)APB \(- \angle\)QPB \(= 90^\circ - \theta\).
**A pair of congruent angles :** \(\angle\)APQ and \(\angle\)BPR, because both measure \(90^\circ - \theta\).
(\(\angle\)APB and \(\angle\)QPR are also congruent, both being right angles.)

**Given :** line \(l \parallel\) line \(m\) and line \(n \perp\) line \(l\).
**To prove :** line \(n \perp\) line \(m\).
**Proof :** line \(n\) intersects line \(l\), and line \(l \parallel\) line \(m\), so line \(n\) is a transversal of line \(l\) and line \(m\).
line \(n \perp\) line \(l\) is given, so the angle line \(n\) makes with line \(l\) is \(90^\circ\).
That angle and the angle line \(n\) makes with line \(m\) on the same side are corresponding angles, and corresponding angles formed by a transversal of two parallel lines are congruent.
\(\therefore\) the angle between line \(n\) and line \(m\) is also \(90^\circ\).
\(\therefore\) line \(n \perp\) line \(m\).

\(\angle x\) and the angle of \(130^\circ\) are opposite angles formed by the two intersecting lines.
\(\therefore \angle x = 130^\circ\)
\(\angle y\) and the angle of \(50^\circ\) are opposite angles formed by the two intersecting lines.
\(\therefore \angle y = 50^\circ\)
Now \(\angle x\) and \(\angle y\) are the interior angles formed on the same side of the transversal of line \(l\) and line \(m\), and
\(\angle x + \angle y = 130^\circ + 50^\circ = 180^\circ\)
If the interior angles formed on the same side of a transversal are supplementary, then the two lines are parallel ..... interior angles test.
\(\therefore\) line \(l \parallel\) line \(m\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives "x = 1260", which is not a possible angle measure. With y : z = 3 : 7 and the interior-angle relation y + z = 180, we get y = 54 and z = 126, and then x = 180 - 54 = 126. The key carries one extra zero: the answer is 126 degrees.]

Line CD \(\parallel\) line EF and line QP is their transversal, so \(\angle y\) and \(\angle z\) are interior angles on the same side of the transversal and are therefore supplementary.
\(\therefore \angle y + \angle z = 180^\circ\)
It is given that \(y : z = 3 : 7\), so let \(\angle y = 3k\) and \(\angle z = 7k\).
\(\therefore 3k + 7k = 180^\circ\)
\(\therefore 10k = 180^\circ\), so \(k = 18^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle y = 3 \times 18^\circ = 54^\circ\) and \(\angle z = 7 \times 18^\circ = 126^\circ\)
Line AB \(\parallel\) line CD with the same transversal, so \(\angle x\) and \(\angle y\) are also interior angles on the same side.
\(\therefore \angle x + \angle y = 180^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle x = 180^\circ - 54^\circ = 126^\circ\)
(The same value follows from AB \(\parallel\) EF, where \(\angle x\) and \(\angle z\) are corresponding angles.)

Line \(q \parallel\) line \(r\) and line \(p\) is their transversal, and \(a = 80^\circ\) is given.
\(\angle a\) and \(\angle\)e are corresponding angles.
\(\therefore \angle\)e \(= \angle a = 80^\circ\)
\(\angle\)f and \(\angle\)e form a linear pair on line \(r\).
\(\therefore \angle\)f \(= 180^\circ - 80^\circ = 100^\circ\)
\(\angle\)g and \(\angle\)e are opposite angles formed by the intersecting lines \(r\) and \(p\).
\(\therefore \angle\)g \(= \angle\)e \(= 80^\circ\)
So \(f = 100^\circ\) and \(g = 80^\circ\).

**Given :** line AB \(\parallel\) line CF and line BC \(\parallel\) line ED.
**To prove :** \(\angle\)ABC \(= \angle\)FDE.
**Proof :** line AB \(\parallel\) line CF and line BC is their transversal.
\(\therefore \angle\)ABC \(= \angle\)BCF ..... alternate angles ..... (I)
line BC \(\parallel\) line ED and line CF is their transversal.
\(\therefore \angle\)BCF \(= \angle\)FDE ..... corresponding angles ..... (II)
From (I) and (II),
\(\angle\)ABC \(= \angle\)FDE
(This is the same principle as Practice set 2.1 Q4 : two angles whose arms are parallel to each other are congruent.)

**Given :** line PS is a transversal of line AB \(\parallel\) line CD, meeting them at Q and R; ray QX, ray QY, ray RX and ray RY are angle bisectors.
**To prove :** \(\square\)QXRY is a rectangle.
**Proof :** line AB \(\parallel\) line CD and line PS is their transversal.
\(\therefore \angle\)AQR \(+ \angle\)QRC \(= 180^\circ\) ..... interior angles on the same side ..... (I)
ray QX bisects \(\angle\)AQR and ray RX bisects \(\angle\)QRC.
\(\therefore \angle\)XQR \(+ \angle\)XRQ \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)AQR \(+ \dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)QRC \(= \dfrac{1}{2}(180^\circ) = 90^\circ\)
In \(\Delta\)QXR, the sum of all three angles is \(180^\circ\).
\(\therefore \angle\)QXR \(= 180^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ\)
By exactly the same argument on the other side, \(\angle\)AQR is replaced by \(\angle\)BQR and \(\angle\)QRC by \(\angle\)QRD, giving \(\angle\)QYR \(= 90^\circ\).
Next, \(\angle\)AQR \(+ \angle\)BQR \(= 180^\circ\) ..... angles in a linear pair
\(\therefore \angle\)XQY \(= \angle\)XQR \(+ \angle\)RQY \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)AQR \(+ \dfrac{1}{2}\angle\)BQR \(= \dfrac{1}{2}(180^\circ) = 90^\circ\)
Similarly, from \(\angle\)QRC \(+ \angle\)QRD \(= 180^\circ\) we get \(\angle\)XRY \(= 90^\circ\).
So all four angles of \(\square\)QXRY measure \(90^\circ\).
A quadrilateral whose all four angles are right angles is a rectangle.
\(\therefore \square\)QXRY is a rectangle.
